Full text

Abstract

Meat consumption in high-income countries exceeds recommendations. Because meals are often shared, conversations can spark meat reduction, yet advocates often remain silent because persuading carries social costs. Generative AI has proven persuasive and could inform such conversations. Drawing on research on persuasion and reactance, we examined how persuasion and its social costs depend on the source of the strategies and on the medium delivering them. In a preregistered 5 × 2 experiment (N = 521), participants discussed a shared meal with a fictional counterpart, either a chatbot or a text-based script. The counterpart used strategies from the behavioral science literature, a large language model, or a generative agent simulation, or did not argue for meat reduction (neutral and placebo controls). Arguing for meat reduction increased intentions and more than quadrupled the odds of choosing a vegetarian dish in both media; arguing for an unrelated sustainability behavior did not shift choice. Persuasion increased perceived threat to freedom but did not reduce liking of the counterpart. AI-derived strategies persuaded as well as literature-based strategies, at no higher social cost. As predicted, the chatbot incurred higher social costs than the text-based dialogue. Studies of AI-based persuasion should assess social costs alongside persuasiveness.

Introduction

Meat consumption in high-income countries far exceeds health and climate targets.

Adopting the planetary health diet could prevent around 15 million deaths annually and substantially reduce agricultural greenhouse gas emissions (Rockström et al., 2025).

Importantly, people often share meals with others, and those meals are embedded in shared contexts, routines, and relationships (Mata, 2026). Shared meals require joint decisions, and in many households a meat-containing dish is the default (Veen et al., 2023). People who intend to eat less meat are most likely to lapse when eating with family or friends, or with others who eat meat (Laffan et al., 2023). Yet social change spreads through those who raise the subject: small shifts carried by front-runners or moral innovators can push a system past a tipping point (Judge et al., 2024; Nardini et al., 2021). Vegetarians and vegans (hereafter veg*ns), however, often remain silent. They routinely avoid the topic in meat-eating company (Salmivaara et al., 2022) or cite taste or health rather than moral reasons, which spares others the implied reproach (Romo & Donovan-Kicken, 2012); some even eat meat in social situations so as not to out themselves (Rosenfeld & Tomiyama, 2019). Bolderdijk and Cornelissen (2022) show experimentally that morally motivated people are devalued by those who are not, which makes such self-silencing the cheaper option. The bottleneck for meatreduction advocacy in everyday social life is therefore not whether it works, but whether it happens at all. This bottleneck reflects the social costs of persuasion, that is, the negative interpersonal consequences of trying to change another person's behavior. These costs can arise on both sides of the exchange. For the person addressed, persuasion can trigger reactance: a message is experienced as a threat to one's freedom to decide, which manifests in anger and counterarguing (Brehm, 1966; Dillard & Shen, 2005). For the advocate, costs arise when the person addressed restores this freedom by devaluing the source of the message (Zuwerink Jacks & Cameron, 2003). On identity-relevant topics, do-gooder derogation describes this devaluation of morally motivated minorities as a defense against anticipated moral criticism (Minson & Monin, 2012; Monin et al., 2008), and De Groeve et al. (2022) unite both strands in a model of resistance to veg*n advocacy in which derogation and avoidance protect the identity of those addressed. Evidence exists for each step. Thürmer et al. (2022) showed that a fictitious person advocating a plant-based diet was devalued in proportion to the threat participants perceived to their own freedom. Lower social attractiveness of veg*n advocates has been documented by MacInnis and Hodson (2017), and social distance by Vandehei and Perry (2023), whose omnivorous participants reported spending less time with relatives who had recently adopted a plant-based diet; dietary homophily makes such distance consequential (Nezlek et al., 2021). We therefore treat threat to freedom, experienced by the person addressed, and lower social attractiveness and closeness, borne by the advocate, as three facets of the social costs of persuasion. Social costs do not necessarily indicate failure. Persuasion can create dissonance between meat consumption and personal values (Rothgerber, 2020), which can be resolved through reduced meat consumption or through defensive responses such as source derogation; discomfort therefore signals that the message landed, and the question is how it is resolved. Dyads reporting meat-related conflict settled on less meat, not more (Mata et al., 2025), and conflict has been read as a signal of a transition under way rather than of its failure (Judge et al., 2024; O'Neill et al., 2019). What ends advocacy is not friction in a single conversation but costs that persist into the relationship, and these costs may be overestimated: conversations about political disagreement with strangers are far less unpleasant than anticipated and foster as much connection as agreement (Wald et al., 2024), and people who restrict meat overestimate how negatively meat eaters react to a request for vegetarian food (Laffan & Howard, 2027).

Whether persuasion works is commonly assessed with the constructs of the theory of planned behavior (Ajzen, 1991): attitudes toward eating less meat, subjective norms reflecting the perceived expectations of important others, perceived behavioral control over doing so, and the intention to do so, which together predict behavior. Interventions arguing for meat reduction can shift attitudes, intentions, and consumption, although average effects on behavior are small (Green et al., 2025), and the behavioral science literature offers a stock of strategies for such arguments, among them information about health and environmental consequences, appeals to social norms, taste-focused framing, and empathy-based appeals to animal welfare. Based on this literature, we expected conversations in which a counterpart argues for eating less meat to persuade and, based on research on reactance and derogation, to incur social costs at the same time. The available strategies, however, were validated in the aggregate and in a form fixed before the recipient was known; few were developed for the moment in which one person needs to persuade another over dinner. Strategy choice also shapes costs: appeals for meat reduction can provoke defensive responses depending on how they are framed (Graça et al., 2026; Truelove, 2025), whereas some communicative approaches raise openness toward those who decline meat (Weiper & Vonk, 2021).

Two alternative sources of persuasion strategies have become available with the emergence of generative AI. Large language models (LLMs), AI systems trained on large text corpora to generate human-like language, have out-persuaded lay human debaters in structured debates (Salvi et al., 2025; see also Karinshak et al., 2023), so they may also be able to generate effective strategies for meat reduction. Generative agent simulations, in which several LLM-based agents interact with one another, offer a different approach (Park et al., 2023; Törnberg et al., 2023): they allow low-cost pretests of human interactions at scale that can inform interventions and data collection with humans (Bail, 2024). We therefore drew on strategies extracted from simulated dialogues about meat reduction (Ahnert et al., 2025). Both AI approaches face the same limitation: neither is based on direct evidence of behavioral effects in humans. LLMs optimize for plausible text, and simulations reproduce the underlying model's assumptions about human interaction, whereas strategies from the literature have been evaluated against observed behavior. Based on this reasoning, we expected literature-based strategies to persuade more and to incur lower social costs than AIderived strategies.

LLMs can also deliver persuasion, as chatbots that respond to whatever a person writes (Lin et al., 2025; Salvi et al., 2025); a brief conversation with an LLM, for instance, weakened participants' commitment to eating meat (Karakaş & Jaeger, 2025). Such adaptivity may matter: a counterpart who takes up the objection actually raised can answer it rather than pre-empt it, and arguments that people elaborate themselves in an exchange carry more weight than arguments they receive (Nisbett & Spaiser, 2023). People also respond to language-capable technology much as they respond to human partners (Reeves & Nass, 1996; see Buder et al., 2025), and current models are often judged to be human (Jones & Bergen, 2024). These findings suggest that a chatbot persuades more than a text-based dialogue that delivers the same strategies along a fixed script. Whether adaptivity also raises social costs is theoretically less clear. A counterpart who responds to one's own objections may threaten one's freedom more than a scripted exchange, and if people treat language-capable systems as social actors, the social costs of persuasion should arise with them too. Conversely, no relationship is at stake with an AI, which could make devaluing it unnecessary, although AI establishes closeness mainly when it is labeled as human (Kleinert et al., 2026). Following the social-actor account, we expected chatbot delivery to incur higher social costs.

Research Gaps and Hypotheses

Three gaps follow from this literature. First, persuasion and its social costs are rarely measured in the same study: work on meat-reduction communication, including first studies of conversations with LLMs (Karakaş & Jaeger, 2025), reports effects on attitudes, intentions, or choices, whereas work on reactance and do-gooder derogation documents how advocates are evaluated. It is therefore unknown whether effective persuasion comes at a social cost. Most of this work, moreover, examines messages addressed to an audience rather than conversations in which two people decide something together. Second, if costs arise, it is unclear whether they are specific to meat or arise whenever one is the target of persuasion.

Third, LLMs can serve both as a source of persuasion strategies and as their communication medium, but the two roles have rarely been separated, and whether a chatbot and a scripted text-based dialogue are equivalent ways of delivering the same strategies has rarely been tested. We addressed these gaps in a preregistered experiment in which participants decided with a fictional counterpart what to cook for a shared meal. We formulated hypotheses where the literature reviewed above supports a directional prediction and research questions where it does not: RQ1. Does conversational advocacy for meat reduction persuade, and does it incur social costs?

H1a. Conversations in which the counterpart argues for eating less meat (persuasive communication) produce more persuasion than conversations without such arguments: more favorable attitudes, stronger intentions, stronger subjective norms, higher perceived behavioral control, and a higher probability of choosing a vegetarian dish.

H1b. Persuasive communication also incurs higher social costs than conversations without such arguments: a stronger threat to the freedom of the person addressed and lower social attractiveness of, and closeness to, the counterpart.

RQ2.

Are the effects of persuasive communication specific to meat-related content, or do they also arise when the counterpart argues just as insistently for an unrelated sustainability behavior? (no directional hypothesis)

RQ3. Does the source of the persuasion strategies-the behavioral science literature or AIaffect persuasion and social costs?

H2a. Literature-based strategies are more persuasive than AI-derived (LLM-generated and simulation-derived) strategies.

H2b. Literature-based strategies incur lower social costs than AI-derived strategies.

RQ4. Does the communication medium-an adaptive chatbot or a text-based dialogue following a fixed script-affect persuasion and social costs?

H3a. Chatbot interactions are more persuasive than text-based dialogues delivering the same strategies.

H3b.

Chatbot interactions incur higher social costs than text-based dialogues delivering the same strategies.

RQ5. Do the effects persist after 1 week, and are they moderated by attitudes toward AI? ≈ 0.14 at α = .05; we oversampled to offset expected exclusions. Prolific participants were paid at a rate of £16.08 per hour for the main study and £13.98 per hour for the follow-up; participants recruited through academic, personal, and professional networks received no financial compensation.

Of the 826 participants who began the study, 174 did not complete it, almost entirely before or at the start of the chat interaction and unrelated to condition. Among the 652 completers, 33 did not meet the meat-consumption criterion and 66 failed the comprehension check (11 met both), and a further 43 were excluded because a configuration error in the chatbot application delivered the literature-based script irrespective of the assigned condition; the error was identified during data collection, corrected, and the affected cases replaced.

This yielded an analytic sample of N = 521, with 50 to 54 participants per cell, slightly exceeding the preregistered target of 500; a sensitivity power analysis for the achieved sample is reported with the results. The sample averaged 41.3 years of age (SD = 13.4; 54.7% male, 45.1% female, 0.2% nonbinary) and 5.25 meat-eating days per week (SD = 1.72), and 88.1% were recruited via Prolific. Prolific participants were invited to a follow-up 1 week later on a first-come, first-served basis: in the first wave, participation was capped at the first 120 respondents, of whom 111 belonged to the analytic sample; second-wave participants were invited after the sample extension until the preregistered follow-up target was reached, adding 14. The follow-up sample thus comprised 125 participants (24.0% of the analytic sample), and follow-up participation was unrelated to communication strategy or medium (ps ≥ .330). A complete breakdown of exclusions and non-completion is provided in Supplement G. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Mannheim (EK Mannheim 96/2025), and all participants provided informed consent at the start of the study.

Design and Intervention

The study used a 5 × 2 between-subjects design with assessments before and after a chat intervention and at a 1-week follow-up (Figure 1). In all 10 conditions, participants took part in the same fictional scenario: deciding together with a fictional conversational counterpart what to cook for a shared meal. Participants were informed that the counterpart was fictional but were instructed to imagine talking to a new friend; no deception was involved. All conditions followed a common five-phase conversational structure-building interpersonal connection, exploring food preferences and the personal meaning of food, introducing condition-specific content, transitioning to the joint meal decision, and closing warmly-and differed in the content of the third phase, which carried the manipulation. In the four conditions in which the counterpart pursued a persuasive goal (the three persuasive conditions and the placebo control), it was instructed to remain in this phase until the participant had sent at least four messages; the neutral control contained no such rule.

Instruction content for the remaining phases was matched in function across conditions, though not verbatim in wording (Supplement E).

The first factor, communication strategy, had five levels. In three persuasive conditions, the counterpart argued for meat reduction using strategies from different sources: a review of behavioral-science evidence (literature-based), generation by GPT-4o from the same task description (LLM-generated), and annotated dialogues between two Llama 3.3 70B generative agents (simulation-derived; Ahnert et al., 2025; see Supplement E). We refer to this distinction as strategy source, to the LLM-generated and simulation-derived strategies jointly as AI-derived, and to the conversations in these three conditions as persuasive communication. The two control conditions isolate different components of the manipulation: the neutral control holds the conversational format constant while removing persuasion entirely, and the placebo control holds both format and persuasive intent constant while replacing the topic with an unrelated pro-environmental behavior, namely reducing packaging waste. Comparing the persuasive conditions with the neutral control therefore captures the combined effect of being persuaded and of the meat-reduction content, whereas the comparison with the placebo control isolates the contribution of the content itself.

The second factor, communication medium, had two levels: chatbot interactions, in which participants exchanged messages with an AI-based counterpart in real time (GPT-5mini, accessed via the OpenAI API), and text-based interactions, in which participants worked through the same content as a branching dialogue: at each turn they chose among preset replies or typed a reply themselves, and the counterpart's turns followed a predefined decision tree. The text-based dialogue is therefore not a static vignette but a scripted interaction, which makes it a conservative comparison for the chatbot: the two media differ in how adaptively the counterpart responds rather than in whether participants interacted at all.

Measures

Figure 1 shows which measures were assessed at which time point. Unless noted otherwise, items were answered on 7-point scales and scale scores were computed by averaging, with higher values indicating stronger endorsement of the construct. Reliability statistics for all measures are reported in Supplement A.

Persuasion was operationalized through four theory of planned behavior constructs, assessed at all three time points, and through behavioral choice. Attitudes toward reducing meat consumption were assessed with four semantic differential items and subjective norms with four items on friends, family, health experts, and colleagues (both Berndsen & van der Pligt, 2004); intentions with three items on white, red, and processed meat (Graça et al., 2015); and perceived behavioral control with two items (Wyker & Davison, 2010). Internal consistency was good to excellent for attitudes, intentions, and subjective norms (α = .77-.96), whereas perceived behavioral control, measured with two items, showed only modest interitem correlations (r = .35-.40), so results for this construct should be interpreted with corresponding caution. Behavioral choice was coded in both media with one annotation procedure. In the chatbot conditions, the meal decision was coded from the conversation logs as a vegetarian dish, a meat-containing dish, or no concluded decision; in the text-based conditions, the dish participants named first was coded as vegetarian or meat-containing.

Coding was performed by an open-weight instruction-tuned language model (google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it), blind to condition, and verified against independent manual coding (κ = .75 for the chatbot meal outcome, 85% exact agreement; κ = .69 for the type of meal in 40 randomly selected conversations coded by a second human rater blind to condition). The same rater also coded whether the counterpart raised meat reduction and which of the 13 instructed strategies it used; the same language model, given the coding scheme with clarified definitions but no examples and blind to condition, then applied it to all first-wave chatbot conversations (Supplement I). The coding rules, the flag for dishes that could be prepared either way, and the documented revisions to the coding scheme are reported in Supplement I.

Meat consumption was assessed at baseline and follow-up with a single item from the GESIS Panel (GESIS, 2020), recoded into days per week (see Supplement F). Social costs were assessed immediately after the intervention with three indicators: threat to freedom (four items; Dillard & Shen, 2005), the social attractiveness of the counterpart (seven items; Thürmer et al., 2022), and social closeness (seven items; Monin et al., 2008). The composite is the mean of z-scored threat to freedom and reverse-scored attractiveness and closeness, so that higher values indicate greater social costs. Threat to freedom correlated only modestly with attractiveness and closeness (r = -.30 and -.25), which were closely related to each other (r = .77); because the facets responded differently to the manipulations, we report facet-level contrasts alongside the preregistered composite.

Communication quality comprised immersion (two items) and affect, assessed with a six-item short form of the PANAS (Watson et al., 1988); positive and negative affect formed distinct subscales and were analyzed separately.

We further assessed age, gender, political orientation (left-right self-placement from 0 to 10, and 14 issue positions from the Social and Economic Conservatism Scale; Everett, 2013), and, in the chatbot conditions and before the interaction, three single items on perceptions of artificial intelligence-self-assessed competency, attitude toward AI, and perceived impact on daily life-taken from the Perceptions on AI by the Citizens of Europe questionnaire (PAICE; Scantamburlo et al., 2025), which assess distinct constructs (α = .64) and were therefore analyzed separately.

For the comprehension check (preregistered as a manipulation check), administered immediately after the intervention, participants selected all applicable statements from four descriptions of the interaction. The check counted as passed only if participants simultaneously endorsed that the goal had been to agree on a dish for a joint cooking session and rejected both that the chat had been with a real person and that the interaction had mainly discussed unrelated topics such as sports or travel. Participants who did not meet this criterion were excluded. Note. Strategies are summarized from the Phase 3 instructions; verbatim instructions for all conditions are reproduced in Supplement E, and complete prompts are available in the Zenodo repository (see Code Availability). Behavioral choice was coded in both media: from the meal decision reached in the chatbot conversations, and from the dish named first in the text-based conditions (Supplement I). Cell sizes refer to the analytic sample.

Analytic Strategy

All analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.4.1; R Core Team, 2024). For outcomes assessed before and after the intervention, we estimated baseline-adjusted linear models with the post-intervention score as the dependent variable and the corresponding baseline score, communication strategy, communication medium, and their interaction as predictors. For social costs and communication quality, assessed only after the intervention, we estimated the same models without a baseline covariate. Omnibus effects were tested using Type III sums of squares with sum-to-zero contrast coding, which is appropriate given the unequal cell sizes (n = 50 to 54) and the inclusion of the interaction term. Behavioral choice was analyzed with logistic regression using the same planned contrasts, separately by medium: among chatbot participants whose conversation reached a meal decision, and among text-based participants, for 257 of whom a dish could be coded. The medium contrast was estimated in a joint model adjusting for the strategy contrasts. Two preregistered sensitivity analyses used all chatbot participants: an intention-to-treat specification coding unconcluded conversations as not vegetarian, and a multinomial model treating the three-category conversation outcome as the dependent variable.

All tests were two-tailed with α = .05. Because the five contrasts reported below were specified a priori and each corresponds to a preregistered hypothesis, a preregistered planned contrast without directional prediction (LLM-generated vs. simulation-derived strategies), or the comparison of the two control conditions, they were tested without correction for multiple comparisons; the preregistration reserved alpha adjustment for post hoc comparisons.

Because H1a spans four self-report constructs, we note where a contrast would not remain significant after Bonferroni correction across them. Standardized effect sizes (d) are contrast estimates divided by the standard deviation of the outcome. Equivalence tests for the strategy-source contrasts (two one-sided tests) were not preregistered and are reported as exploratory. Missing data were handled using available cases. Model diagnostics, heteroscedasticity-robust estimates, recruitment-source and covariate sensitivity analyses are reported in Supplement D, and deviations from the preregistration in Supplement H.

Statistics and Reproducibility

The target sample size was set by an a priori power analysis before data collection (G*Power 3.1; Faul et al., 2009) and extended under a preregistered amendment with a fixed stopping rule; no analysis informed when data collection stopped. Exclusion criteria were preregistered and applied before analysis (Supplement G). Participants were assigned to conditions at random by the survey software and were not informed about the other conditions or the comparative aim of the study; behavioral choice was coded by a language model blind to condition and verified against human coding (Supplement I). The study was conducted once, but the behavioral effect was tested independently in two media within it.

All tests were two-tailed with α = .05. The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework on 21 November 2025, before data collection began (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/N9BCS); an amendment specifying the second recruitment wave, its stopping rule, and its allocation was registered on 7 October 2026. Data and code to reproduce every reported result are listed under Data Availability and Code Availability.

Large language models (ChatGPT, OpenAI; Claude, Anthropic) were used to assist with writing and checking the analysis code and with editing the manuscript text; the authors reviewed and verified all code and text and take full responsibility for the content.

Results Randomization and Descriptive Results

There was no evidence that the five communication strategy conditions or the two medium conditions differed in age, gender, political orientation, baseline meat consumption, or any baseline theory of planned behavior construct (all ps ≥ .096; Supplement B).

Descriptive statistics for all outcomes and outcome distributions are reported in Supplement C. As specified in the preregistered amendment, we repeated the planned contrasts with collection wave as a covariate, and no conclusion changed. The wave × condition interaction, which tests whether condition effects differed between the two recruitment waves, was significant for subjective norms, F(9, 500) = 3.14, p = .001, and for social costs, F(9, 501) = 2.27, p = .017, but not for intentions, attitudes, or perceived behavioral control (ps ≥ .269).

Given small second-wave cells (n = 6 to 18), we note that the effects of persuasive communication on intentions and social costs and of medium on social costs were each significant within the first wave alone (n = 418).

Effects of Persuasive Communication on Persuasion and Social Costs (RQ1, H1)

Table 1 reports all preregistered contrasts; Figure 2 shows behavioral choice and social costs by condition, and all contrasts as standardized differences.

Persuasion (H1a)

Persuasive communication raised intentions to reduce meat consumption relative to the control conditions (Figure 2C), although the effect was small, b = 0.18, d = 0.11, and would not remain significant after Bonferroni correction across the four constructs (p = .019 > .0125). The effect on attitudes pointed in the same direction but reached significance only in a sensitivity model adjusting for baseline meat consumption (p = .040; Supplement D).

There was no evidence of an effect on subjective norms or perceived behavioral control.

Among the psychological constructs, H1a was therefore supported for intentions only.

The behavioral evidence pointed in the same direction, and it replicated across both media. Among the 124 chatbot conversations that concluded with a meal decision, vegetarian dishes were chosen more often after persuasive than after control conversations, b = 1.51, SE = 0.43, OR = 4.52, 95% CI [1.95, 10.50], p < .001. In the text-based conditions, where nearly every participant named a dish, the same contrast yielded b = 1.56, SE = 0.28, OR = 4.78, 95% CI [2.78, 8.21], p < .001 (Figure 2A). Both preregistered sensitivity analyses for the chatbot conditions reproduced the effect: the multinomial specification (see Conversation Completion) and the intention-to-treat specification, which counts every unconcluded conversation as not vegetarian, OR = 2.33, 95% CI [1.10, 4.91], p = .026. The text-based replication carries particular weight, because participants named a dish regardless of whether the exchange converged on a joint decision, so the outcome is not conditioned on a variable that the manipulation itself affected.

Social Costs (H1b)

Social costs were higher in the persuasive than in the control conditions, b = 0.34, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [0.21, 0.47], p < .001, d = 0.43 (Figure 2C), and the effect was unchanged when recruitment source or demographic covariates were included (Supplement D). H1b was supported. The three facets, however, did not move together. The effect was carried entirely by threat to freedom, which rose by 1.53 scale points, d = 0.98, p < .001, whereas the counterpart's social attractiveness, d = 0.01, p = .946, and participants' wish for closeness, d = -0.04, p = .623, showed no evidence of change. Because the threat-to-freedom items partly register that an influence attempt took place (e.g., "tried to influence me"), part of this effect reflects recognition of the attempt rather than a cost in the narrower sense.

Specificity of the Effects (RQ2)

The placebo control differs from the neutral control only in being addressed persuasively, not in being addressed about meat. The preregistered comparison between the two control conditions was null for every persuasion outcome, including behavioral choice, and for the social-cost composite (all ps ≥ .142; Table 1). One facet was an exception: the placebo counterpart raised threat to freedom relative to the neutral control, b = 0.56, SE = 0.18, p = .002, indicating that persuasive intent alone was sufficient to threaten participants' freedom. Compared with the placebo control alone, vegetarian choices remained more likely after persuasive conversations in both media (chatbot: OR = 4.25, 95% CI [1.26, 14.31], p = .020; text-based: OR = 5.30, 95% CI [2.67, 10.53], p < .001), and threat to freedom was again higher, b = 1.25, SE = 0.15, p < .001. For intentions and attitudes, by contrast, there was no evidence of a difference from the placebo control (p = .325 and p = .554); the H1a effect on intentions arose relative to the neutral control (p = .006). The behavioral effect and most of the increase in threat to freedom are therefore specific to meat-reduction content, whereas the shift in self-reported intentions cannot be separated from the persuasive exchange as such.

Effects of Strategy Source (RQ3, H2)

Restricted to the three persuasive conditions, there was no evidence that literaturebased, LLM-generated, and simulation-derived strategies differed in persuasion, F(2, 303) = 0.35, p = .705, for intentions and F(2, 303) = 1.74, p = .177, for attitudes, or in social costs, F(2, 304) = 1.61, p = .201. For social costs, however, strategy source interacted with medium, F(2, 304) = 11.96, p < .001: simulation-derived strategies were considerably more costly when delivered by the chatbot than in the text-based dialogue (see below). Neither planned contrast reached significance for any psychological outcome (all ps ≥ .072) or for behavioral choice in either medium (all ps ≥ .137; Table 1); change-score analyses supported the same conclusion.

Because absence of evidence is not evidence of equivalence, we conducted a sensitivity power analysis. With the achieved sample, the omnibus test of communication strategy retained 80% power for f = 0.15 and the medium contrast for d = 0.25, both close to the preregistered targets. The comparisons among the three strategy sources, however, drew on smaller subsets and retained 80% power only for d = 0.34 and d = 0.39. Exploratory equivalence tests (two one-sided tests) ruled out differences of d = 0.40 between literature-based and AI-derived strategies on all five outcomes and of d = 0.25 on the four persuasion constructs; for social costs, equivalence at d = 0.25 could not be established, p = .068, nor could equivalence of the two AI-derived sources at d = 0.40, p = .074. H2a and H2b were therefore not supported, and the comparisons were sensitive enough to detect moderate but not small differences between strategy sources.

Effects of Communication Medium (RQ4, H3)

There was no evidence that communication medium affected persuasion on any theory of planned behavior outcome (all ps ≥ .265; Table 1), and H3a was not supported for the psychological outcomes. For behavioral choice, the medium contrast was significant in the opposite direction to the hypothesis: vegetarian dishes were less likely in the chatbot than in the text-based conditions, b = -0.71, SE = 0.24, OR = 0.49, 95% CI [0.30, 0.79], p = .003 (Table 1). Because the two media also differ in how the outcome was elicited-a decision negotiated with the counterpart in the chatbot conditions versus a dish named by the participant in the text-based conditions-and because the chatbot estimate is restricted to concluded conversations, this difference should not be read as a medium effect alone. Social costs, in contrast, were higher in the chatbot than in the text-based conditions, as predicted, b = 0.30, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [0.17, 0.43], p < .001, d = 0.38 (Figure 2B and 2C), and the difference held with recruitment source and with demographic covariates (both ps < .001; Supplement D). H3b was supported. Unlike the effect of persuasive communication, the medium effect ran through all three facets: participants rated the chatbot counterpart as less socially attractive, d = -0.31, wished for less closeness with it, d = -0.39, and felt their freedom more threatened, d = 0.21 (all ps ≤ .005). The communication strategy × communication medium interaction was significant for social costs, F(4, 511) = 6.51, p < .001, η² = .05, but for none of the persuasion outcomes. The chatbot-text difference was ₚ largest for simulation-derived strategies, b = 0.90, SE = 0.15, p < .001, absent for literature-based strategies, b = -0.14, SE = 0.15, p = .341, and intermediate in the remaining conditions (b = 0.21 to 0.27, ps = .067 to .143). It did not depend on the simulation condition alone: the medium effect held when that condition was excluded, b = 0.15, SE = 0.07, p = .040, and within the two control conditions, b = 0.24, SE = 0.10, p = .020.

Communication Quality (Secondary Outcome)

Immersion was higher in all four conditions with a persuasive goal than in the neutral control, both in the persuasive-versus-control contrast, b = 0.30, SE = 0.10, p = .004, and in the placebo-versus-neutral contrast, b = 0.48, SE = 0.16, p = .003. Because the strategy × medium interaction was significant for this outcome, F(4, 511) = 2.87, p = .023, these averaged contrasts should be interpreted with caution, and because the same four conditions also produced longer chatbot conversations (Supplement D), immersion cannot be attributed to persuasive communication alone. There was no evidence that participants' positive or negative affect differed between communication strategies or communication media (all ps ≥ .140; with affect before the interaction as a covariate, all ps ≥ .056), so neither persuasive communication nor the chatbot's higher social costs came with a more negative emotional experience of the conversation.

Exploratory Analyses

Persistence at Follow-Up (RQ5)

At the 1-week follow-up (n = 125), the persuasive-versus-control contrast was positive but not significant for intentions, b = 0.35, SE = 0.24, p = .153, and also nonsignificant for the remaining theory of planned behavior constructs and for self-reported meat consumption (all ps ≥ .175). Meat consumption declined across all conditions alike, from 5.48 to 4.72 days per week. Because follow-up participation was restricted to Prolific participants on a first-come, first-served basis, this subsample is not representative of the full sample; the only contrast that reached significance at follow-up, higher intentions after LLM-generated than after simulation-derived strategies, b = 0.69, SE = 0.34, p = .048, is uncorrected and reported in Supplement D.

Conversation Completion

Of the 259 chatbot conversations, 135 ended without a meal decision. The rate was 22.2% in the neutral control condition and between 46.0% and 64.7% in the four other conditions, χ²(4, N = 259) = 29.64, p < .001, and conversation length followed the same pattern (neutral control: M = 18.9 messages, SD = 6.5; LLM-generated: M = 30.7, SD = 16.7).

In a multinomial model, which treats the three possible conversation outcomes (vegetarian decision, meat-containing decision, no decision) jointly, persuasive communication shifted outcomes away from a meat-containing decision, b = -0.91, SE = 0.21, p < .001, and toward a vegetarian decision, b = 0.60, SE = 0.26, p = .021, whereas the shift toward no decision was smaller and not significant, b = 0.32, SE = 0.20, p = .107. This pattern cannot be attributed unambiguously to persuasion: the placebo condition was among those with the most unconcluded conversations, and the four conditions with a persuasive goal instructed the counterpart to remain in Phase 3 until the participant had sent at least four messages, whereas the neutral control did not (Supplement E).

Attitudes Toward AI as a Moderator (RQ5)

Among chatbot participants, a more favorable attitude toward AI predicted lower social costs, F(1, 249) = 31.28, p < .001, without interacting with communication strategy, F(4, 249) = 1.26, p = .288, and did not significantly predict post-intervention intentions, F(1, 248) = 3.32, p = .070. The association was stronger for attractiveness and closeness (r = .35 and .38) than for threat to freedom (r = -.13). Self-assessed AI competency and perceived impact of AI on daily life were not significantly associated with either outcome (all ps ≥ .058). As uncorrected tests in a single-medium subsample, these patterns are exploratory.

Discussion

This study examined whether conversational advocacy for meat reduction can persuade without social costs, and whether AI can help. Persuasive communication increased intentions and vegetarian choices (RQ1, H1a) and incurred social costs (H1b), but these costs took the form of a threat to the freedom of the person addressed rather than devaluation of the counterpart. The effect on choice was specific to meat-related content, whereas the increase in intentions could not be distinguished from that produced by a counterpart arguing for an unrelated behavior (RQ2). We found no evidence that strategies from the behavioral science literature, an LLM, or a generative agent simulation differed in persuasion or social costs (RQ3, H2a, H2b). The chatbot did not persuade more than the text-based dialogue (RQ4, H3a) but incurred higher social costs (H3b). Together, these results address the three gaps identified at the outset.

Regarding RQ1, persuasive communication persuaded as predicted in H1a, but mainly in what participants chose rather than in what they reported. The increase in intentions was small, in line with the modest average effects of meat-reduction interventions (Green et al., 2025), and there was no reliable change in attitudes, subjective norms, or perceived behavioral control. Behavioral choice, by contrast, shifted substantially and consistently in both communication media. That choices moved more than stated intentions reverses the usual intention-behavior gap (Sheeran & Webb, 2016) and fits the premise that a shared meal is decided in the conversation rather than before it (Mata, 2026), as in parent-child dyads, in which raising sustainability arguments went along with less meat on the shared plate (Mata et al., 2025). Dialogues with LLMs have shifted beliefs (Costello et al., 2024) and attitudes toward meat (Karakaş & Jaeger, 2025); the present results extend such effects to a behavioral choice. Regarding RQ2, the placebo control shows that the behavioral effect was driven by meat-related content rather than by engagement in a persuasive exchange, whereas the small increase in intentions was not specific to this content.

Persuasive communication also incurred social costs, as predicted in H1b, but only on one side of the exchange. Participants felt that their freedom to decide was threatened-the first step of reactance (Brehm, 1966; Dillard & Shen, 2005)-but did not find the counterpart less attractive or want less closeness with it, suggesting that source derogation (Zuwerink Jacks & Cameron, 2003) did not occur. A likely reason lies in what the counterpart did not do: do-gooder derogation targets morally motivated minorities whose stance implies reproach (Minson & Monin, 2012), and in the closest precursor to this study the advocate was introduced as vegan (Thürmer et al., 2022). Our counterpart claimed no dietary identity, was instructed to remain non-evaluative, and argued for a shared dish rather than a moral position -advocacy that may be easy to decline without resenting the person behind it. Threat to freedom nonetheless remains a cost for the person addressed. Meat-reduction interventions elicit it even when they offer practical suggestions (Graça et al., 2026), the placebo counterpart elicited it to a lesser extent, and part of it likely reflects that the items register the persuasion attempt itself; it was not accompanied by more negative affect. When a counterpart threatens the freedom of the person addressed without being liked less, the relational cost that keeps advocates silent does not arise. This converges with evidence that people overestimate the costs of engaging with opposing views (Dorison et al., 2019), of discussing disagreement (Wald et al., 2024), of deeper conversation (Kardas et al., 2022), and of requesting vegetarian food (Laffan & Howard, 2027). If the costs that keep advocates silent (Bolderdijk & Cornelissen, 2022) are similarly overestimated, the bottleneck identified at the outset-whether advocacy happens at all-may be easier to overcome than it appears.

Regarding RQ3, we found no evidence that the source of the strategies mattered, so H2a and H2b were not supported. Strategies generated by an LLM persuaded as well as strategies drawn from the evidence, and exploratory equivalence tests ruled out moderate differences between literature-based and AI-derived strategies, although small differences cannot be excluded. This extends evidence that LLMs produce persuasive content (Karinshak et al., 2023; Salvi et al., 2025) to a comparison with curated behavioral science. Simulationderived strategies did not persuade more and, when delivered by the chatbot, incurred the highest social costs, which may reflect how imperfectly generative agents reproduce human social responses (Bisbee et al., 2024) or a loss of what made the strategies effective when they were extracted from the simulated dialogues. Conversation coding confirmed the topic manipulation but could not reliably verify individual strategies (Supplement I), so the comparison concerns the strategies as instructed.

Regarding RQ4, the communication medium affected social costs but not persuasion.

Contrary to H3a, the chatbot's adaptivity did not make the counterpart more persuasive, paralleling evidence that tailoring messages to the individual adds little persuasive power (Hackenburg & Margetts, 2024; Hackenburg et al., 2025). As predicted in H3b, however, the chatbot incurred higher social costs, and unlike persuasive communication, it also lowered the social attractiveness of, and closeness to, the counterpart, in the control conditions as well. Responses attributed to AI are valued less than identical responses attributed to people (Rubin et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2024), and AI establishes closeness mainly when labeled as human (Kleinert et al., 2026). The cost may therefore reflect perceptions of the chatbot itself rather than the content of its messages. That it was largest for simulation-derived strategies was not predicted and warrants replication. Vegetarian choices were less frequent in the chatbot conditions, but because the two media elicited the choice differently, we do not attribute this difference to adaptivity.

Regarding RQ5, no effects were detectable at the 1-week follow-up; durable effects of behaviors embedded in social routines. Among chatbot participants, more favorable attitudes toward AI went along with lower social costs but did not moderate the effects of persuasive communication.

This study has several strengths. It was preregistered and powered for the targeted effect sizes, separated persuasive intent from meat-related content through two control conditions, and coded behavior blind to condition with human verification. Because the behavioral effect held across two communication media, strategies from three sources, and a sample from three countries drawn from the population that advocacy targets, in a scenario that reproduces how shared meals are negotiated, it is unlikely to depend on a single implementation. Because participants had no reason to trust or please their counterpart, the persuasive effects are, if anything, conservative estimates for people who know each other.

The study also has limitations. First, in all conditions with persuasive or placebo content, the counterpart was instructed to stay with this content for a minimum number of exchanges, whereas the neutral control had no such rule. Because the placebo control shared this rule, the comparisons that establish content specificity are unaffected, but conversation completion and immersion cannot be interpreted as effects of persuasion. Second, more chatbot than text-based participants failed the comprehension check and were excluded, so the chatbot sample may over-represent conversations that stayed on task. Third, the increase in intentions was small and would not remain significant after correction for the four theory of planned behavior constructs tested. Fourth, the LLMs that generated and simulated strategies were trained on large amounts of online text and have likely encountered research on meat reduction; AI-derived strategies may therefore partly reproduce the literature, which would narrow differences between strategy sources. Finally, participants chose a dish for a hypothetical meal with an imagined counterpart, so the costs measured are costs attributed to someone without a shared history. Whether the absence of derogation extends to existing relationships is therefore a key question for future research.

These findings have implications for theory and research. Routinely measuring social costs alongside persuasion would allow researchers to identify which strategies achieve persuasion at the lowest social cost, rather than focusing solely on persuasive effectiveness.

Theoretically, the dissociation between threat to freedom and liking qualifies the link between reactance and source derogation (De Groeve et al., 2022; Thürmer et al., 2022). Our interpretation-that source derogation requires a persuader whose stance implies moral reproach-could be tested by varying whether the same arguments are presented by a selfidentified, morally motivated vegetarian. Research on AI-based interventions should likewise separate AI as a source of persuasion strategies from AI as a communication medium, as the two had different effects in the present study. Future work should examine repeated conversations in existing relationships and compare the costs anticipated by advocates with those reported by the people they address.

The findings also have practical implications. For intervention design, LLMs can generate persuasion strategies at a fraction of the cost of a literature review without a detectable loss in persuasive effectiveness, and a text-based dialogue achieved the same selfreported persuasion as a chatbot at lower social cost. For advocates, the message is encouraging: speaking up influenced what others chose and threatened their freedom without making the speaker less likeable, a social cost that may be smaller than advocates anticipate (Laffan & Howard, 2027; Wald et al., 2024), particularly when advocacy proposes a shared choice rather than asserting a moral position. While a single conversation may change only a single meal, repeated conversations with different people may gradually produce more stable change, much as consistent minorities shift majority views over time (Bolderdijk & Jans, 2021).

In sum, persuasion can shift meat-related choices in the moment, at the social cost of a threat to the freedom of the person addressed rather than diminished regard for the person persuading. Conversations about shared meals may thus offer a promising starting point for reducing meat consumption in high-income countries, with potential benefits for both climate change mitigation and the prevention of avoidable deaths. do not imply a nonsignificant difference; tests of all planned differences are reported in Table 1.

Supplement D: Sensitivity and Robustness Analyses

This section reports the sensitivity and robustness analyses referenced in the main text: the preregistered sensitivity analyses for behavioral choice, model diagnostics, recruitment source, collection wave, additional covariates, attitudes toward AI as a moderator, subgroup analyses, and the exploratory follow-up analyses. None of these analyses altered the conclusions reported in the main text.

Behavioral Choice: Preregistered Sensitivity Analyses

Because the meal decision could only be coded for chatbot conversations that reached a conclusion, and because reaching a conclusion is itself a post-treatment outcome, we specified two sensitivity analyses using all 259 chatbot participants. Under an intention-to-treat specification coding unconcluded conversations as not resulting in a vegetarian choice, the persuasive-versus-control contrast remained significant, OR = 2.33, 95% CI [1.10, 4.91], p = .026. A multinomial logistic model with no decision as an additional outcome category showed that persuasive conversations made a meat-containing decision less likely (b = -0.91, SE = 0.21, p < .001) and a vegetarian decision more likely (b = 0.60, SE = 0.26, p = .021), whereas the effect on reaching no decision was not significant (b = 0.32, SE = 0.20, p = .107); estimates are on the latent scale of the multinomial model. In the text-based conditions, where 257 of 262 participants named a dish, no comparable selection problem arises.

Differential Conversation Completion

Of the 259 chatbot conversations, 135 (52.1%) ended without a meal decision. The proportion was 22.2% in the neutral control condition and ranged from 46.0% (literature-based) to 64.2% (placebo) and 64.7% (LLM-generated and simulation-derived) in the four conditions with a persuasive goal, χ²(4, N = 259) = 29.64, p < .001. Conversation length showed a corresponding pattern, with the fewest messages in the neutral control condition (M = 18.9, SD = 6.5) and the most in the LLM-generated condition (M = 30.7, SD = 16.7). Because the four conditions with a persuasive goal instructed the counterpart to remain in Phase 3 for at least four participant messages, whereas the neutral control did not, differences in completion and conversation length cannot be attributed unambiguously to persuasive content (see Supplement E).

Ambiguous Dishes

The annotation flagged dishes that could be prepared either with or without meat (e.g., "pizza", "curry", "lasagne" without further specification). Under the coding scheme these were classified as meat-containing unless the text marked them as meat-free, which is the conservative option.

Excluding the flagged cases strengthened the persuasive-versus-control contrast in both media: in the chatbot conditions to b = 1.98, SE = 0.61, OR = 7.26, 95% CI [2.18, 24.21], p = .001 (34 of 124 cases excluded), and in the text-based conditions to b = 1.84, SE = 0.32, OR = 6.28, 95% CI [3.39, 11.64], p < .001 (42 of 257 excluded). The conclusion reported in the main text therefore does not depend on how ambiguous dishes are treated; the primary analysis reports the more conservative estimate.

Model Diagnostics

Generalized variance inflation factors (Fox & Monette, 1992), computed with sum-to-zero contrast coding, indicated no multicollinearity in the five confirmatory linear models (adjusted GVIF = 1.00-1.01). Cook's distance identified no influential cases, with maximum values of D = 0.13 (intentions), 0.05 (attitudes), 0.07 (subjective norms), 0.07 (perceived behavioral control), and 0.02 (social costs). Breusch-Pagan tests indicated heteroscedasticity in the perceived behavioral control model, p < .001, and the social-cost model, p = .007, but not in the intentions, attitudes, or subjective-norms models (ps ≥ .255). Recomputing all planned contrasts with heteroscedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errors changed no conclusion: every contrast that was significant under ordinary least squares remained significant, and none became significant.

For the logistic models of behavioral choice, which include a single categorical predictor, Cook's distance identified no influential cases (maximum D = 0.04 in the chatbot and 0.01 in the textbased conditions), and coefficient estimates and standard errors remained within conventional bounds (maximum |b| = 0.97, maximum SE = 0.42), giving no indication of quasi-separation. The models correctly classified 68.5% (chatbot) and 68.9% (text-based) of choices, against base rates of 62.9% and 56.0% for the more frequent outcome.

Recruitment Source

Recruitment source was not confounded with communication strategy, χ²(4, N = 521) = 4.76, p = .313, or communication medium, χ²(1, N = 521) = 0.81, p = .369. Prolific and self-recruited participants nevertheless differed on several baseline characteristics.

Values are group means. Welch's t tests were used throughout. Political orientation is the 0-10 left-right self-placement; higher values indicate a more conservative position.

Including recruitment source as a covariate did not alter any conclusion. The persuasive-versuscontrol contrast remained significant for intentions, b = 0.18, SE = 0.08, p = .018, and for social costs, b = 0.34, SE = 0.07, p < .001, and the medium effect on social costs held, b = 0.31, SE = 0.07, p < .001. Recruitment source itself predicted social costs, F(1, 510) = 4.10, p = .043, with self-recruited participants reporting higher social costs, but none of the theory of planned behavior constructs (all ps ≥ .098).

Collection Wave

As specified in Amendment 1, we repeated all planned contrasts with collection wave as a covariate. No conclusion changed: the persuasive-versus-control contrast remained significant for intentions, b = 0.18, p = .020, and for social costs, b = 0.35, p < .001, the medium effect on social costs held, b = 0.31, p < .001, and no other contrast reached significance (all ps ≥ .063). The wave × condition interaction was significant for subjective norms, F(9, 500) = 3.14, p = .001, and for social costs, F(9, 501) = 2.27, p = .017, but not for intentions, F(9, 500) = 1.24, p = .269, attitudes, F(9, 500) = 0.58, p = .813, or perceived behavioral control, F(9, 500) = 0.63, p = .768. Because the second-wave cells were small (n = 6 to 18), we re-estimated the planned contrasts in the first wave alone (n = 418). The effects of persuasive communication on intentions, b = 0.18, p = .043, and on social costs, b = 0.35, p < .001, and the medium effect on social costs, b = 0.28, p < .001, were each significant within the first wave. In the first wave, social costs were additionally lower after LLM-generated than after simulation-derived strategies, b = -0.29, p = .014, a contrast that was not significant in the full sample (p = .092). No contrast on subjective norms was significant in either analysis.

Additional Covariates

The preregistration specified that models would control for relevant covariates including baseline meat-eating frequency. As a sensitivity analysis, we reestimated all five confirmatory models with baseline meat consumption as an additional covariate, and then additionally with age, gender, and political orientation. Baseline meat consumption predicted post-intervention attitudes, F(1, 509) = 8.93, p = .003, and perceived behavioral control, F(1, 509) = 5.24, p = .022, but not intentions, subjective norms, or social costs (all ps ≥ .052). Its inclusion left the pattern of planned contrasts unchanged, except that the persuasive-versus-control contrast for attitudes reached significance, b = 0.21, SE = 0.10, p = .040 (without the covariate, p = .063). Adding age, gender, and political orientation left all conclusions unchanged and slightly strengthened the persuasive-versus-control contrasts (intentions, p = .011; attitudes, p = .025; social costs, p < .001) and the medium effect on social costs (p < .001).

Attitudes Toward AI as a Moderator

Among chatbot participants (n = 259), we tested whether the three single items on perceptions of AI moderated the effect of communication strategy on intentions and social costs. The three items were only modestly intercorrelated, r = .28-.46. A more favorable attitude toward AI predicted lower social costs, F(1, 249) = 31.28, p < .001, without interacting with communication strategy, F(4, 249) = 1.26, p = .288, and did not significantly predict post-intervention intentions, F(1, 248) = 3.32, p = .070. The association was stronger for social attractiveness and closeness (r = .35 and .38) than for threat to freedom (r = -.13). Self-assessed AI competency and perceived impact of AI on daily life were not significantly associated with either outcome (all ps ≥ .058). These are uncorrected exploratory tests in a single-medium subsample and should be treated as hypothesis-generating.

Subgroup Analyses

We examined whether the absence of average differences among strategy sources could reflect opposing effects in demographic subgroups, comparing the youngest with the oldest quartile of participants, crossed with gender. Among participants in the three persuasive conditions in the youngest (≤ 31 years) and oldest (≥ 51 years) quartile (n = 155), no interaction of strategy source with age group, gender, or both reached significance for intentions, attitudes, or social costs (all ps ≥ .052). The cells of this analysis are small, so it can detect only large moderating effects.

Exploratory Follow-Up Analyses

At follow-up (n = 125), one exploratory contrast among the three persuasive conditions reached conventional significance: follow-up intentions were higher in the LLM-generated than in the simulation-derived condition, b = 0.69, SE = 0.34, p = .048. The contrast between literature-based and AI-derived strategies was not significant for any construct (all ps ≥ .142). The LLM-versussimulation contrast rests on the reduced follow-up sample, was not corrected for multiple comparisons, and was not mirrored in the corresponding post-intervention analysis; it is reported for completeness and should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than as evidence for differences among strategy sources.

Follow-up participants did not differ from non-participants on baseline theory of planned behavior constructs or age (all ps ≥ .217); they reported slightly more frequent baseline meat consumption (5.48 vs. 5.17 days per week), p = .052. Follow-up participation was unrelated to communication strategy, χ²(4, N = 521) = 4.61, p = .330, or communication medium, χ²(1, N = 521) = 0.05, p = .815.

Supplement E: Interaction Design and Prompts

All 10 conditions used the same five-phase conversational structure and the same fictional scenario. In the chatbot conditions the counterpart was implemented with GPT-5-mini (OpenAI); in the text-based conditions participants worked through the same content as a branching dialogue, choosing among preset replies or typing their own, with the counterpart's turns following a predefined decision tree. This section reproduces the shared conversational frame, the condition-specific instructions for Phase 3, which constitute the experimental manipulation, and the condition-specific elements outside Phase 3. The five complete system prompts are available in the Zenodo repository.

Shared Conversational Frame

The role instruction was identical in all five prompts: "You are not an assistant. You are playing the role of a fictional person who will cook together with the participant, with the task of deciding on a meal." Participants sent the first message; the counterpart followed the phase structure from its second message onward.

Phase 1: Building Interpersonal Connection.

The counterpart responded warmly to the participant's opening message and asked about the emotional experience they wanted from the shared meal. Ingredients and cooking details were excluded at this stage.

Phase 2: Exploring Preferences and the Meaning of Food.

The counterpart asked open questions about the participant's relationship with food and, in the four conditions involving meat-related or packaging-related content, about what food or meat represented to them personally. No dishes were suggested.

Phase 3: Condition-Specific Content. This phase carried the manipulation and is reproduced verbatim for all five conditions in Table S9.

Phase 4: Meal Decision.

The counterpart summarized the participant's reflections in a neutral, non-judgmental way and moved to the joint meal decision. Evaluative or approving language toward the participant, such as expressions of pride or praise for a choice, was prohibited in order to avoid social reinforcement that would differ systematically across conditions.

Phase 5: Closing. Once a decision was reached, or after the participant had sent seven to ten messages, the counterpart thanked the participant, acknowledged the shared decision, and stated that this part of the study was finished. The three instructions constituting this phase, including the suggested closing formulation, were verbatim identical across all five prompts.

Four cross-cutting rules appeared in every prompt: never provide recipes, ingredient lists, or cooking steps; never behave like an assistant or expert; keep replies short, warm, personal, and human; and vary sentence openings and conversational style so as not to produce recognizably templated responses. The instruction on varying phrasing was verbatim identical across all five prompts.

Table S9 Verbatim Phase 3 Instructions by Communication Strategy Condition Condition Phase 3 instruction Literaturebased Use ONLY the following evidence-based strategies to guide the participant toward reflecting on and reducing meat consumption: Highlight health benefits of reducing meat. Combine health and environmental appeals.

Include emotional appeals regarding animal welfare. Communicate that many people are reducing their meat intake. Tailor your messages to the participant's personal motivations and concerns. LLMgenerated Use ONLY these strategies: Highlight health benefits. Make tasty vegetarian alternatives emotionally tangible. Appeal to empathy and environmental Condition Phase 3 instruction awareness. Promote a step-by-step approach instead of full abstinence. Leverage shared values and relatable role models. Simulationderived Use ONLY these strategies: Build on the participant's own ideas to establish common ground. Use rhetorical questions to encourage engagement. Suggest gradual meat reduction. Highlight benefits of the proposed direction. Give short examples to make reduction tangible (without ingredients). Neutral control Present possible general directions neutrally (e.g., "lighter vs. richer," "warm vs. fresh," "traditional vs. twist"). Be open and accepting of ANY preference the participant expresses. Stay curious about their motivations without influencing them. NO persuasion of any kind. Placebo control Use ONLY these strategies: Highlight positive impact of choosing unpackaged ingredients for health and safety. Show convenient and attractive low-waste alternatives. Highlight environmental impact of packaging waste (not diet). Encourage small, achievable changes. Connect to shared values and social norms about reducing waste. DO NOT mention meat, vegetarianism, diet, animal welfare, or food-related environmental issues.

Note. Bullet formatting has been rendered as running text; wording is otherwise verbatim. Instructions prohibiting the counterpart from naming the strategies to the participant and from moving to meal planning during this phase accompanied each of the four persuasive and placebo blocks.

Condition-Specific Elements Outside Phase 3

Three further differences between the prompts fall outside Phase 3 and are documented here for transparency.

First, the goal statement in each preamble necessarily named the respective objective: meat reduction in the three persuasive conditions, explicit neutrality in the neutral control ("You do NOT attempt to influence the participant's meat consumption, dietary habits, or any health/environment-related decisions"), and packaging waste in the placebo control. This difference is inherent to the manipulation. Second, the cross-cutting rules listed above were supplemented in two conditions by contentspecific prohibitions. The neutral control additionally prohibited environmental, health, animalwelfare, and social-norm arguments as well as technical cooking descriptions; the placebo control prohibited any link to diet, meat, or health beyond packaging. These additions serve to keep each condition within its intended content boundaries.

Third, and most consequential for interpretation, the four conditions with a persuasive goal (the three persuasive conditions and the placebo control) instructed the counterpart to remain in that phase until the participant had sent at least four messages, and correspondingly to begin discussing meal ideas only after that point. The neutral control contained no such dwell rule and no gating condition on Phase 4, and could therefore proceed to the meal decision as soon as the participant's preferences were clear. This asymmetry is a plausible partial explanation for two patterns reported in the main text: the neutral control produced the shortest conversations and had by far the highest rate of concluded meal decisions, whereas the placebo condition, which carried the dwell rule but no meat-related content, patterned with the three persuasive conditions.

The prompts additionally differed in verbosity outside Phase 3. Instruction content for Phases 1, 2, and 4 was matched in function across conditions, but the wording was not verbatim identical: the literature-based prompt stated these phases most extensively, including example formulations, whereas the simulation-derived and placebo prompts stated them most concisely. The full prompts in the Zenodo repository allow this variation to be inspected directly.

Text-Based Dialogue Networks

The text-based conditions implemented the same phases as a fixed branching dialogue. The counterpart's messages were scripted; participants replied by choosing among preset options, completing sentences by dragging items into gaps, or typing free text, and the counterpart's next message depended on the option chosen at the first branching point. The complete networks of all five conditions are documented in the Zenodo repository.

Two features of the networks differed between conditions. First, in the opening turn participants proposed dishes by dragging them from a predefined list. In the three persuasive conditions, this list contained only meat-containing dishes, which allowed the counterpart to respond with its meat-reduction proposal; in the neutral and placebo control conditions, it also contained vegetarian dishes (e.g., vegetable lasagna, mushroom risotto). Second, the dish analyzed as behavioral choice was elicited at the end of the dialogue in the persuasive and placebo conditions, as the first of up to three meal suggestions, but earlier in the neutral control, where participants typed the dish they had in mind after the opening turn. The first difference, if anything, made vegetarian choices more likely in the control conditions and therefore works against the persuasive-versus-control contrast. The second does not affect the comparison with the placebo control, which used the same elicitation as the persuasive conditions and also showed more vegetarian choices after persuasive conversations (see main text).

Derivation of the Simulation-Derived Strategies

The simulation-derived strategies were extracted from simulated dialogues about meat reduction between two generative agents based on Llama 3.3 70B (Ahnert et al., 2025; code: https://github.com/dess-mannheim/MeatlessAgents). A persuader agent was instructed to convince a recipient agent to eat less meat; each dialogue ran for ten rounds, and after each round the recipient agent answered the intention items of the theory of planned behavior questionnaire. In total, the simulation comprised 270 dialogues with nine recipient personas.

Persuader messages were annotated for the persuasion strategy they used, yielding 29 distinct strategies. To this end, Llama 3.3 70B described the persuasion strategy of each persuader message in free text; these descriptions were embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and clustered with BERTopic, and the most representative description of each of the 29 clusters was retained as the strategy. For each strategy, the change in the recipient agent's meat-reduction intention following the messages that used this strategy was computed over the first four rounds of dialogue, because meat-reduction intention remained largely constant in later rounds. The change was min-max normalized within each recipient persona and then averaged across personas.

The five strategies with the largest normalized change were included in the counterpart's instructions for the simulation-derived conditions: building on the recipient's idea to establish common ground (79 annotated messages; normalized change = 0.64), using rhetorical questions to encourage engagement (20; 0.63), suggesting a gradual reduction in meat consumption (305; 0.62), highlighting the benefits of the proposed option (110; 0.61), and providing specific examples to make the idea more tangible (139; 0.59). The ranking of all 29 strategies is available in the Zenodo repository.

Supplement F: Recoding of the Meat Consumption Measure

Meat consumption was assessed with a single item asking on how many days per week participants usually eat meat. The item offered 13 ordered response options whose spacing does not correspond to equal intervals on the underlying frequency scale. Because the question itself is framed in days per week, responses were converted to that metric for analysis and reporting, so that higher values indicate more frequent consumption.

Options 1 and 2 (several times a day and once a day) both correspond to seven days per week; the item distinguishes intensity within a day, which the question does not ask about. Options below one day per week were converted using an average of 4.345 weeks per month. Option 12 (less than once per month) has no defined frequency and was assigned a nominal value of 0.12 days per week, corresponding to approximately one occasion every two months.
