Non-Completion

Because 174 of 826 participants (21.1%) did not complete the study, we examined when noncompletion occurred and whether it was related to experimental condition.

Table S12 Point of Non-Completion in the Questionnaire Point at which participation ended n % of noncompleters Before responding to the consent page 95 54.6 After consent, before condition assignment 2 1.1 After condition assignment, before the post-intervention questionnaire 67 38.5 During the post-intervention questionnaire 10 5.7 Note. n = 174 non-completers. Categories are derived from which questionnaire sections contain responses.

Non-completion was concentrated at the very beginning of the study: more than half of the noncompleters left before responding to the consent page. Among the 77 non-completers who had already been assigned to a condition, non-completion was evenly distributed across the 10 conditions, χ²(9) = 10.53, p = .309, indicating that the intervention itself did not differentially drive participants to discontinue.

Non-completion differed markedly by recruitment channel. Among participants recruited via Prolific, 14.5% (92 of 633) did not complete the study, compared with 42.5% (82 of 193) of participants who accessed the study through an open link shared via academic, personal, and professional networks, χ²(1) = 69.50, p < .001. The overall non-completion rate is thus largely attributable to the open recruitment link, where opening the study without beginning it carries no cost, rather than to features of the study itself.

Supplement H: Deviations From Preregistration

Several aspects of the reported analyses depart from the preregistration; we document them here for transparency.

Hypothesis Numbering.

The preregistration stated two hypotheses with lettered subcomponents. For clarity, we renumbered them so that each hypothesis corresponds to one planned contrast and the suffixes a and b consistently denote persuasion and social costs, respectively. H1a corresponds to preregistered H1d, H1b to H1c, H2a to H1b, H2b to H1a, H3a to preregistered H2a, and H3b to H2b. No hypothesis was added, dropped, or altered in content. To structure the report, the main text additionally groups the analyses under five research questions; these introduce no new hypotheses. RQ1, RQ3, and RQ4 correspond to the preregistered hypotheses, RQ2 to the preregistered comparison of the two control conditions, and RQ5 to preregistered exploratory analyses (follow-up and perceptions of AI).

Exclusion Criteria.

The preregistration specified four data-quality exclusion criteria (insufficient engagement, speeding, invalid responding, and manipulation-check failure). We refer to the preregistered manipulation check as a comprehension check, because it assessed whether participants had understood the scenario rather than whether the manipulation had been effective; its content and pass criterion are unchanged. Exclusions were implemented on the basis of the meat-consumption eligibility criterion, speeding, and comprehension-check failure. The engagement and invalid-responding criteria were not applied as separate filters because the comprehension check functionally subsumed them: passing required participants to correctly judge three separate statements about a conversation they had just completed, which inattentive or undifferentiated responding would not reliably achieve. The speeding criterion was applied but removed no participants beyond those already excluded for not completing the study.

Outcome Presentation Order.

The preregistration listed vegetarian choice as the first primary outcome, followed by the theory of planned behavior constructs. We report the psychological outcomes before behavioral choice, reflecting the narrative logic of first establishing attitudinal and social-cost effects.

Theory of Planned Behavior Composite.

The preregistration specified a standardized composite index (mean of z-scored intentions, attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control) as the primary continuous outcome. We report the four constructs separately in the main text to preserve theoretical interpretability, since they showed divergent patterns of results. As a robustness check, we additionally estimated the preregistered composite. The omnibus effect of communication strategy was F(4, 510) = 2.37, p = .051, η² = .02, and the ₚ planned contrast comparing persuasive with control conditions was significant, b = 0.07, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14], p = .024, consistent with the pattern observed for intentions.

Facet-Level Reporting of Social Costs.

The preregistration specified the social-cost composite, which remains the confirmatory outcome for H1b, H2b, and H3b. Because threat to freedom correlated only modestly with social attractiveness and closeness (r = -.30 and -.25) and the facets responded differently to the manipulations, we additionally report facet-level contrasts in the main text and in Figure 2C.

Equivalence Tests.

Equivalence tests (two one-sided tests) for the strategy-source contrasts were not preregistered and are reported as exploratory.

Meat Consumption Coding.

The preregistration did not specify how the 13-point meatconsumption item would be coded. Because the item asks about days per week, we recoded responses into days per week so that higher values indicate more frequent consumption (see Supplement F).

Perceptions of AI.

The preregistration specified trust in artificial intelligence, assessed only among chatbot participants, as an exploratory moderator. The items were indeed administered only in the chatbot conditions. The instrument administered in our materials, labeled Perceptions on AI and taken from the Perceptions on AI by the Citizens of Europe questionnaire (PAICE; Scantamburlo et al., 2025), departs from this in three respects. First, none of its items assesses trust: participants rated their self-assessed competency regarding AI, their attitude toward AI and its applications, and the extent to which AI already affects their daily life. Second, all three items used 5-point rather than the preregistered 7-point response scales. Third, the three items assess distinct constructs-self-rated knowledge, evaluation, and perceived personal relevance-rather than indicators of a single latent variable. Interitem correlations were accordingly modest, r = .28 to .46, and a composite reached only α = .64. We therefore analyzed the three items separately rather than averaging them.

Operationalization of Affect.

The preregistration described a single affect rating as part of perceived communication quality and a separate negative affect covariate, without specifying the item source. Our materials assessed affect using a six-item short-form PANAS, which yielded two distinct, highly reliable subscales rather than a single undifferentiated rating. We therefore analyzed positive and negative affect separately rather than forcing a single composite.

Sample Extension (Amendment 1).

The first recruitment wave ended with unequal cell sizes below the preregistered target of about 50 per cell. Before data collection resumed, a second wave was registered as Amendment 1, with a fixed stopping rule and allocation weighted toward the cells furthest from the target: the randomization urn was preset so that the first assignments of the second wave reproduced the number of participants missing per cell, after which allocation reverted to equal probabilities. At the start of the second wave, a configuration error in the chatbot application delivered the literature-based script irrespective of the assigned condition. Affected cases were identified by comparing the condition assigned in the survey with the condition delivered according to the application log, a rule fixed before results were inspected, and were excluded and replaced (Supplement G). The same error had occurred on a pilot day before the first wave (28 November 2025); these cases were excluded on the same grounds, so the first wave contributes 418 cases to the analytic sample rather than the 428 analyzable cases reported in the amendment. Wave was included as a covariate and as a moderator in sensitivity analyses without altering the conclusions (Supplement D). The follow-up target of 120 usable cases was reached by inviting second-wave Prolific participants on a first-come, first-served basis, which added 14 cases to the 111 from the first wave; because the second-wave follow-up was capped at the number of cases still needed, follow-up rates are not comparable between waves.

Alpha Adjustment.

The preregistration stated that adjustments would be applied if multiple post hoc comparisons were conducted. All contrasts reported in the main text were specified a priori, and no adjustment was applied.

Supplement I: Annotation of Behavioral Choice

Behavioral choice was coded with two annotation pipelines that share one codebook: a conversation-level pipeline for the chatbot conditions, which codes the meal outcome from the full transcript, and a text-level pipeline for the text-based conditions, which codes the dish participants named. Both were run with an open-weight instruction-tuned language model (google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it). The model saw only the transcript or the dish text, never the condition name or the system prompt the counterpart had received, so the coding is blind to condition. Each variable was coded in a separate call; the model returned a probability for each answer option, and the code is the most probable option. Each call also returned a short explanation and a verbatim citation, and citations were checked against the transcript afterwards.

Coding Rules for Dish Choice

The same rules apply in both media. In the text-based conditions, where participants could name up to three dishes, the dish named first is coded. Fish and seafood count as meat. Dishes whose standard recipe contains meat (e.g., spaghetti bolognese) count as meat-containing unless the text marks them as meat-free. A meat-free dish to which one diner adds meat for their own portion counts as meat-containing. Texts that name no dish are excluded from the analysis; this applied to 5 of 262 text-based participants. Each entry additionally received a flag for dishes that could be prepared either way, which is used in the sensitivity analysis reported in Supplement D.

Human Verification

Two sets of manual codes serve as verification. For the chatbot conditions, one rater had coded the meal outcome of all conversations manually; agreement with the model was κ = .75 (85% exact agreement) for the final meal outcome and κ = .68 (82%) for the dish the conversation started from. A second rater had coded 40 conversations on the full scheme; agreement with the model was κ = .63 (82%) for whether a meal decision was reached and κ = .69 (80%) for the type of meal. The same rater also coded whether the counterpart raised meat reduction and which of the 13 instructed strategies it used. Model and human agreed closely on whether meat reduction was raised (κ = .90, 95% agreement), and across all first-wave chatbot conversations the model coded it in 105 of 107 persuasive and in none of 88 control conversations of the analytic sample. Agreement on the individual strategies was considerably lower (Table S13), mainly because the model coded generic conversational moves such as tailoring to the participant or building on their ideas in nearly every conversation, including those in the control conditions. The strategy codes are therefore not used to characterize the conditions and are reported here for transparency only.

Revisions to the Coding Scheme

Setting up the pipelines made several ambiguities in the original coding descriptions explicit, and each was resolved with a documented clarification before annotation. The thresholds for whether the counterpart and the participant engaged in dialogue were defined in terms of observable message content. "The selected meal" was defined as any dish proposed in the conversation, so that meat talk could be coded even when no meal was agreed. The category "partially meat-free" was removed, so that the type of meal is coded as meat-free or meat-containing in both media. Drop-out is judged from the last message of the counterpart, because a completed conversation ends with a scripted closing message. Rhetorical questions were distinguished from ordinary questions about preferences, and the instruction to give short examples was restricted to examples of eating patterns rather than recipes. The full annotation instructions, the documented clarifications and the annotation code are available in the Zenodo repository.

Supplement A: Internal Consistency of Multi-Item Measures

Internal consistency was computed for all multi-item scales at each time point at which they were assessed. For two-item scales, the interitem correlation is reported instead of Cronbach's α, given the known instability of α for two-item measures (Eisinga et al., 2013).
